sections.text: The ballad begins with epithets of praise for King Kitekere.
During the night, a spirit medium is roused unwillingly from a sleep by his youngest wife.
They argue.
The elder wives ask the medium about the contents of his dream but receive a curt rebuff.
The wives help prepare the spirit medium for his journey to the king.
The spirit medium travels, eventually meeting a ferryman to whom he indicates his mission and provides payment.
The spirit medium travels on through several landmarks.
At the outskirts of the palace compound, the guards he meets question the feasibility of his mission, and he answers them, demonstrating his knowledge of court life.
On being asked, the guards tell the spirit medium that the king is in a grove playing the game of mankala. The spirit medium proceeds towards the palace and sees warriors practicing military skills.
He meets the guardian of the royal court and provides gifts. The spirit medium proceeds to an audience with the king.
He greets the king and presents his prophecy that warns about a particular warrior. The king receives the information favorably.
An alarm is heard, and guesses as to its origin in the hunt are offered and dismissed with arguments based on conventions of poetic praise.
Finally, a cowherd arrives and with great emotion reports a cattle raid to the king.
The king responds, recognizing the truth of the prophecy by repeating part of it. Then the cowherd reports the results of an attack on several villages.
The king responds first with emotion then with heroic gestures that foretell action.
The king prepares for battle first by consulting diviners. Then he gives orders to household servants to prepare provisions.
The warriors present at court chant their self-praise to prepare for battle.
The king sets out. He pauses to comment on some monkeys as symbols of the ruling dynasties of other kingdoms Another warrior chants his praise.
The king summons particular warriors and names the battalions each should serve with.
The king attacks Kihanja kingdom. Scenes of battle are described. The army moves on and the king orders particular villages attacked.
After victorious battle, several warriors chant their self-praise.
The army travels further into Kihanja, attacks other settlements, and crosses into Ihangiro Kingdom. Another scene of men in battle is described.
The king of Ihangiro is heard to utter words of fear and awe for Kitekere and to order that tribute be paid him. Royal women of Ihangiro comment on Kitekere's manliness.
Kitekere decides to stay temporarily in Ihangiro, receives tribute from the king there, and threatens further attack. His men counsel peace.
The army stays to harvest its millet and then returns home. The self-praise of victorious warriors is heard again.
In a coda, the singer comments on the punishment of the miscreant and envisions the descendants of Kitekere walking back to Kyamutwara Kingdom.
